Kazuma Asogi was a student at Imperial Yumei University studying law, while also serving as a defense attorney. Due to his exemplary academic achievements, he was also chosen to study abroad in the British Empire towards the end of Japan's Meiji era. After his best friend Ryunosuke Naruhodo was put on trial for the murder of John H. Wilson and subsequently acquitted, Kazuma requested that he accompany him to Britain.

Kazuma Asogi was born the only son of Genshin Asogi and hailed from a long line of swordsmen. When he was eight years old, his father departed for the Great British Empire as part of a student exchange program.

Six years into his stay in London, Genshin would be arrested for the death of Klint van Zieks. Needing a scapegoat for the series of murders known as the Professor Killings, Mael Stronghart approached Genshin while he was in jail with a proposal: should he consent to being framed as the Professor, he would be allowed to return home to his son Kazuma and the rest of his family. Genshin agreed. Years later Stronghart would describe Kazuma as Genshin's "only weakness."

Genshin was permitted to compose a will, of which he wrote three pages. In the first two pages, Genshin accepted his fate and requested that all of his personal effects were to be sent to his son in Japan upon his death. However, the last page contained hidden instructions for Kazuma to find the evidence that would unveil the truth of the Professor Killings (Klint van Zieks's Will). The existence of the last page had been concealed by Stronghart.

After his fraudulent execution, Genshin was betrayed and murdered by Seishiro Jigoku after Enoch Drebber stumbled upon him escaping his grave. Months after Genshin's death, once Jigoku and Yujin Mikotoba had returned to Japan, Mikotoba visited the Asogi estate to inform Kazuma and his mother of Genshin's passing, telling them that he had died due to a fatal illness.

One day, though, Kazuma received a hateful letter from what he would later presume to be a relative of one of the Professor's victims. The letter informed him that his father had been sentenced to death for the killing spree, and cursed the Asogi name. This was the first time Kazuma had ever heard of the Professor Killings. Knowing that Mikotoba had lied out of consideration for his feelings, Kazuma chose not to tell him about the letter, instead showing it Jigoku. Though Jigoku laughed it off, Kazuma was struck by the initial shock on his face. Jigoku's shock and the letter's contents led Kazuma to the realization that there was more to what happened than what he was being told.

A year later after Mikotoba and Jigoku's return from England, Kazuma's mother would pass away from grief. Kazuma states that the death of his mother was when he decided he would someday travel to England and seek out the truth of what happened. The suffering his father's death had caused, and his belief in his innocence, ultimately motivated Kazuma to become a defense attorney and pursue a trip to Great Britain.

After the death of his mother, Kazuma was taken in by Mikotoba and raised alongside his daughter, Susato. Mikotoba funded Kazuma's university education, and continually pushed the government to allow Kazuma to study overseas.
